trackers.name: Bayer Crop Science
trackers.desc: WHAT. The largest seed and agricultural-trait business in the world, formed when Bayer bought Monsanto in 2018 for around $63 billion and retired the Monsanto name. It sells maize, soybean, cotton, vegetable and canola seed under the Dekalb, Asgrow and Seminis brands, licenses its traits to competitors, and sells the glyphosate herbicide those traits are engineered to survive. WHERE IT SITS. At the top. Its traits appear in seed sold by firms that compete with it, so its reach is wider than its market share suggests, and the same company supplies the seed and the chemical the seed is designed for. WHY IT MATTERS. Selling a herbicide-tolerant seed and the herbicide together means the trait creates the market for the chemical. That is a closed loop by design, and it is the single arrangement that shaped modern row-crop agriculture more than any other. The glyphosate litigation Bayer inherited runs to tens of thousands of claims and provisions in the billions — which is the company's own accounting of what the loop cost.

trackers.name: Corteva Agriscience
trackers.desc: WHAT. The agricultural company spun out of the DowDuPont merger in 2019, carrying Pioneer — the oldest and one of the largest seed brands in the world — together with the Dow and DuPont trait portfolios and crop-protection lines. WHERE IT SITS. Second in seed globally, and a major licensor: its traits are grown by farmers who never bought a Corteva bag, and it in turn licenses in from Bayer. The four majors trade traits with each other constantly, which is why they are competitors in name and a shared platform in practice. WHY IT MATTERS. Cross-licensing between the majors means a farmer choosing between brands is often choosing between packages of the same underlying traits. It looks like a market and functions closer to a cartel of technology, without anyone having to agree to anything illegal.

trackers.name: Bayer — investor filings
trackers.desc: WHAT. Bayer's own annual and quarterly reporting, including segment revenue and the litigation provisions. WHERE IT SITS. The company's account of itself, written for people who have money at stake rather than for the public. WHY IT MATTERS. The risk-factor section is the most candid document any of these companies produces. A company will tell shareholders what it will not tell a regulator, because misleading the former is a securities offence. Read it before reading anything the same company publishes about safety.

trackers.name: Corteva — CRISPR licensing framework
trackers.desc: WHAT. Corteva holds or controls a large share of the agricultural CRISPR patent estate, partly through an exclusive arrangement with the Broad Institute, and licenses it out. WHERE IT SITS. Between the academic institutions that hold the foundational patents and every agricultural company that wants to use the technique. WHY IT MATTERS. The technique was developed largely with public research funding, and the right to use it in crops is now controlled commercially. A university spin-out or a national breeding programme in a low-income country wanting to edit a local crop must negotiate with a company that competes with it. That is the enclosure of a method, not of a product.

trackers.name: Ginkgo Bioworks
trackers.desc: WHAT. A synthetic biology company selling organism engineering as a service — clients specify what they want a microbe to produce and Ginkgo designs, builds and tests strains at scale. WHERE IT SITS. A foundry model: it does not own most of the products, it owns the capability to make them, and it sells that capability by the project. WHY IT MATTERS. Selling engineering as a service means capability accumulates in one place while responsibility spreads across dozens of clients. When something goes wrong the client holds the permit and the foundry holds the know-how, and no regulator has a view of the whole pipeline.

trackers.name: Inari Agriculture
trackers.desc: WHAT. A crop-editing company using computational design and multiplex editing to alter yield and resource-use traits in soy, maize and wheat. WHERE IT SITS. In the space opened by editing being treated as outside GMO registration in several jurisdictions — designed for a regulatory route the older technology does not have. WHY IT MATTERS. Companies of this kind exist because of a regulatory decision, not despite one. Where editing has been ruled equivalent to conventional breeding there is no application, no assessment and no register entry, which means no public record that the product exists at all.

trackers.name: Twist Bioscience
trackers.desc: WHAT. A DNA synthesis company using a silicon-chip platform to write genes and oligonucleotide libraries at high volume and low cost. WHERE IT SITS. Upstream of everything. Almost every engineered organism on this map began as a sequence ordered from a company like this one. WHY IT MATTERS. This is where capability is actually gated, and the gate is commercial rather than legal. Synthesis firms screen orders against sequences of concern voluntarily; no government requires it, and a meaningful share of global capacity sits outside the industry's own screening consortium. The most consequential control point in the whole industry is a company policy.

trackers.name: Integrated DNA Technologies (Danaher)
trackers.desc: WHAT. One of the largest suppliers of custom oligonucleotides, gene fragments and CRISPR guide RNAs, owned by the Danaher conglomerate. WHERE IT SITS. The everyday supply line for laboratories worldwide — the routine orders rather than the headline projects. WHY IT MATTERS. Ownership by a diversified industrial conglomerate is worth noticing. Decisions about who may buy synthesised DNA are taken inside a company whose main business is something else entirely, and which faces no biosafety regulator at group level.

trackers.name: Illumina
trackers.desc: WHAT. The dominant supplier of high-throughput DNA sequencing instruments and the consumables they require. WHERE IT SITS. Effectively the infrastructure of genomics. Most large sequencing datasets in existence were generated on its machines. WHY IT MATTERS. The instruments are sold cheaply relative to the consumables they consume, which locks buyers into a proprietary supply chain for the life of the machine. A national genomics programme, an agricultural breeding institute and a hospital all end up dependent on one company's pricing, and that dependency is a design choice rather than an accident.

trackers.name: Addgene
trackers.desc: WHAT. A non-profit plasmid repository that stores and distributes the genetic constructs behind published research, at low cost, to laboratories worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. The circulation layer. When a method is published, the construct that makes it usable generally moves through here. WHY IT MATTERS. Access requires a verified institutional account. That single requirement — repeated across plasmid repositories, cell-line banks and most reagent suppliers — is the largest practical barrier between the public and this technology, and it is rarely mentioned in writing about biotechnology being democratised. The knowledge is open; the materials are not.

trackers.name: Charles River Laboratories
trackers.desc: WHAT. A contract research organisation supplying laboratory animals, running preclinical safety studies, and providing the animal models used across pharmaceutical and biotechnology research. WHERE IT SITS. Both a supplier and a testing house — it breeds and sells the animals and also runs the studies performed on them. WHY IT MATTERS. The safety studies regulators read are commissioned and paid for by the company seeking approval and executed by a contractor that depends on repeat business from that industry. Nobody in that chain is paid by the public. It is a structural conflict rather than an allegation about any particular study.

trackers.name: Labcorp Drug Development (formerly Covance)
trackers.desc: WHAT. One of the largest contract research organisations, running preclinical and clinical studies for pharmaceutical and biotechnology clients worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. The middle of the pipeline. Much of the evidence base a regulator assesses was generated here rather than by the company named on the application. WHY IT MATTERS. Following the contractor rather than the client shows an industry far more concentrated than its company list suggests. Dozens of sponsors, a handful of laboratories actually doing the work.

trackers.name: The Jackson Laboratory
trackers.desc: WHAT. A non-profit that breeds and distributes genetically defined mice, holding thousands of mutant and transgenic strains and shipping worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. The reference source for mouse models. A large share of published mouse research uses strains that originate here, which makes it infrastructure rather than a supplier. WHY IT MATTERS. Standardising the animal standardises the science, and thousands of strains exist because someone needed a specific disease phenotype bred into a living creature and kept alive as a line. The catalogue is the clearest available statement of what the industry does to animals at volume: it is a product list, and every entry is a lineage bred to be ill in a particular way.

trackers.name: Taconic Biosciences
trackers.desc: WHAT. A commercial supplier of genetically modified rodent models, including custom model generation to a client's specification. WHERE IT SITS. The made-to-order end of the animal trade — a company will engineer and breed a line that does not yet exist. WHY IT MATTERS. Custom model generation is genetic engineering sold as a routine service, with the resulting animals treated as a deliverable. There is no register of these organisms comparable to a crop release register, because they are contained — which means the largest volume of engineered vertebrates in the world is also the least publicly recorded.

trackers.name: Envigo / Inotiv
trackers.desc: WHAT. A supplier of research animals and preclinical services, following the acquisition of Envigo's animal business by Inotiv. WHERE IT SITS. Alongside Charles River in the small group of firms supplying most of the world's laboratory animals. WHY IT MATTERS. Consolidation in animal supply means welfare standards across an entire research sector depend on the practices of very few companies, and enforcement actions against those companies have direct consequences for tens of thousands of animals at a time.

trackers.name: Acceligen (Recombinetics)
trackers.desc: WHAT. A company gene-editing cattle and other livestock for traits including heat tolerance and hornlessness, marketed as welfare and productivity improvements. WHERE IT SITS. At the front of the argument that edited livestock should not count as regulated articles, and a beneficiary wherever that argument has won. WHY IT MATTERS. Its hornless cattle line was found to contain unintended bacterial plasmid DNA that the developers had not detected and regulators found later. The animals were presented as a clean, precise edit. That episode is the strongest available evidence that precision claims in this field are claims rather than findings, and it came from the regulator, not from critics.

trackers.name: AquaBounty Technologies
trackers.desc: WHAT. Developer of AquAdvantage salmon, an Atlantic salmon engineered with a Chinook growth-hormone gene to reach market weight faster. The first engineered animal approved for human consumption anywhere. WHERE IT SITS. The precedent case for engineered food animals, cited in every subsequent argument in every jurisdiction. WHY IT MATTERS. Approval took roughly two decades, and the commercial result has been repeated retrenchment and facility closures. The lesson the industry drew was not that the product was wrong but that the regulatory route was too slow — which is why the effort since has gone into getting animals classified as unregulated rather than into getting them approved.

trackers.name: ViaGen Pets & Equine
trackers.desc: WHAT. A commercial cloning service that will clone a customer's dog, cat or horse from a tissue sample, for a published fee. WHERE IT SITS. Entirely outside biosafety regulation — a cloned animal contains no foreign DNA, so most frameworks have nothing to say about it. WHY IT MATTERS. This is the industry operating with no oversight at all, on companion animals, as a consumer purchase. Cloning requires many surrogate pregnancies and produces losses that do not appear in any published figure, because no one is required to publish one. The absence of a register here is not an oversight; it is the design.

trackers.name: Target Malaria
trackers.desc: WHAT. A non-profit research consortium developing gene-drive mosquitoes intended to suppress malaria-transmitting Anopheles populations across sub-Saharan Africa. WHERE IT SITS. The furthest-advanced gene-drive programme in the world, working through partner institutions in Burkina Faso, Uganda and Ghana. WHY IT MATTERS. A gene drive is designed to spread through a wild population and cannot be recalled or confined to a country that consented to it. In August 2025 Burkina Faso sealed the programme's facilities and suspended its activities, days after a non-drive trial release. Whatever the merits of eliminating malaria, the governance question the programme raises is whether any single national approval can be sufficient for an organism engineered to cross borders.

trackers.name: Pivot Bio
trackers.desc: WHAT. A company selling engineered soil microbes that fix nitrogen for cereal crops, applied at field scale as a replacement for part of a farmer's synthetic fertiliser. WHERE IT SITS. Agricultural biologicals — a fast-growing sector applying engineered organisms across millions of acres with far less public attention than engineered seed. WHY IT MATTERS. These are living organisms broadcast into soil in enormous quantity, and soil microbial communities are the least understood ecosystem being altered at that scale. The environmental case made for the product — less synthetic fertiliser — is real. It is also the reason the release is happening faster than the monitoring.

trackers.name: Colossal Biosciences
trackers.desc: WHAT. The best-funded de-extinction venture, working on engineered proxies for the woolly mammoth, thylacine and dodo, and on genetic rescue for living endangered species. WHERE IT SITS. At the intersection of venture capital and conservation, holding the resulting intellectual property. WHY IT MATTERS. What is produced is a modified living species engineered to resemble an extinct one, not a restoration. The deeper effect is rhetorical: if extinction can be presented as reversible, the argued cost of causing it falls. That reframing is already doing work in policy debate, years before any such animal exists, and it is doing it on behalf of a company that would own the result.

trackers.name: Living Carbon
trackers.desc: WHAT. A company engineering poplar and other trees for faster growth and greater carbon accumulation, and planting them on reclaimed and private land. WHERE IT SITS. Where engineered organisms meet carbon markets — the tree is the product and the carbon credit is the revenue. WHY IT MATTERS. Trees are perennial, wind-pollinated, long-lived and frequently planted within their native range, which is the worst possible risk profile for containment. Attaching a carbon-credit revenue stream to planting them creates a financial reason to plant more, faster, and to argue against restrictions — a structural incentive that did not exist when engineered trees were only a research question.

trackers.name: Vertex / CRISPR Therapeutics — Casgevy
trackers.desc: WHAT. The first approved CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia, launched at roughly $2.2 million per patient. WHERE IT SITS. The proof that genome editing works as medicine, and the template for what such medicine costs. WHY IT MATTERS. Sickle cell disease is most prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa and among people of African descent. The first cure for it is priced at a level almost none of the affected population can access, and requires transplant-grade hospital infrastructure. The therapy is real and it works; who it reaches was decided commercially, not scientifically.

trackers.name: ClinicalTrials.gov
trackers.desc: WHAT. The public registry of clinical trials, including gene transfer, gene editing and engineered cell products, with sponsor, phase and site. WHERE IT SITS. The only systematic public record of genetic engineering applied to human beings. WHY IT MATTERS. It records what is being trialled, on whom and where, which makes visible a pattern the industry does not advertise: trial sites and eventual markets are frequently not the same countries. It is also the only place the germline and embryo research boundary can be observed rather than assumed.

trackers.name: Orchid Health
trackers.desc: WHAT. A company offering whole-genome sequencing of embryos before implantation, reporting risk scores across a range of conditions and traits. WHERE IT SITS. The furthest commercial edge of embryo selection — beyond screening for specific disorders and into ranking embryos on probabilistic scores. WHY IT MATTERS. Polygenic scores are weak predictors at the individual level and are derived largely from populations of European ancestry, so they perform worse for everyone else. Selling them as a basis for choosing which embryo becomes a person applies a statistical tool well outside what it can support, to a decision that cannot be revisited. This is where the eugenic question stops being theoretical and becomes a purchase.

trackers.name: CDC ART clinic data
trackers.desc: WHAT. Federally mandated annual reporting of assisted reproductive technology outcomes by clinic in the United States. WHERE IT SITS. Statistics without a statutory clinic regulator behind them. WHY IT MATTERS. The United States has clinic-level numbers and no clinic-level regulator, which is an unusual combination. Reporting exists; enforcement does not. That gap is the shape of the American fertility industry.

trackers.name: Gates Foundation — committed grants database
trackers.desc: WHAT. A searchable record of every grant the foundation has made, with recipient, amount and purpose, including its agricultural development programme. WHERE IT SITS. Among the largest funders of agricultural biotechnology deployment in Africa and South Asia, and a major funder of the institutions that regulate and evaluate it. WHY IT MATTERS. Private philanthropy setting agricultural research priorities for whole regions is governance without an electorate. The foundation publishes its grants, which is more than most funders do — and the published record is what makes the scale of that influence checkable rather than arguable.

trackers.name: DARPA — Biological Technologies Office
trackers.desc: WHAT. The US defence research agency's biology programme, which has funded gene drives, engineered organisms, and human performance and resilience work. WHERE IT SITS. Outside civilian biosafety oversight, in every country that runs an equivalent. WHY IT MATTERS. Military biotechnology is the facet with the least public visibility and the fewest constraints. DARPA at least publishes programme names and funds academic work that appears in the literature, which makes it the most legible example of the least legible part of the industry — and a reminder that equivalents in other states publish nothing at all.

trackers.name: BIO — Biotechnology Innovation Organization
trackers.desc: WHAT. The largest biotechnology trade association, representing over 1,100 companies across more than 30 countries, lobbying on regulation, patents and pricing. WHERE IT SITS. The industry's collective voice, filing on members' behalf so individual firms need not appear. WHY IT MATTERS. Trade associations exist partly so that positions no single company wants attributed to it can still be advanced. Reading BIO's filings on a rule tells you which provisions the industry wants removed, in plainer language than any member company would use in its own name.

trackers.name: ISAAA — GM approval database
trackers.desc: WHAT. The most complete event-level record of GM crop approvals by country, maintained by an industry-supported organisation, together with the annual global adoption figures quoted on all sides of the argument. WHERE IT SITS. An advocacy organisation that happens to keep the best register in the field. WHY IT MATTERS. The database is genuinely useful and the organisation exists to promote adoption. Both are true. Citing an industry source for an industry figure is stronger than citing a critic for one — but the framing around the numbers is written to persuade, and the two should be read differently.

trackers.name: Syngenta Group
trackers.desc: WHAT. Seed and crop-protection company headquartered in Basel, acquired by ChemChina in 2017 for around $43 billion and now inside the Chinese state-owned Sinochem Holdings. Sells maize, soy, vegetable and cereal seed and one of the largest pesticide portfolios in the world. WHERE IT SITS. One of the four, and the only one that is an arm of a state. It combines a European research base, a Chinese owner and a global sales network. WHY IT MATTERS. State ownership removes the levers that work on the others. There is no shareholder resolution to file, no securities regulator to petition, and no proxy vote. Pressure on Syngenta has to run through trade policy or through the countries where it sells — a materially different problem from pressuring a listed company, and one most campaigning is not set up for.

trackers.name: Syngenta — seedcare & seeds portfolio
trackers.desc: WHAT. The company's own product catalogue across field crops and vegetables. WHERE IT SITS. The commercial face of the trait pipeline — what has left the laboratory and reached a bag. WHY IT MATTERS. Catalogues are more informative than press releases. The treatments and traits listed against each variety show what the seed is designed to be used with, which is the practical shape of the input package a farmer is buying into.

trackers.name: Novartis — gene therapy
trackers.desc: WHAT. Manufacturer of Zolgensma, a one-time gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy launched at around $2.1 million per dose, and of the CAR-T therapy Kymriah. WHERE IT SITS. The commercial leading edge of genetic medicine, and the origin of the pricing model the rest of the field follows. WHY IT MATTERS. The science behind these therapies rests heavily on decades of publicly funded research. The pricing puts them beyond every health system outside a handful of wealthy countries. A technology developed with public money, priced so that most of the world cannot reach it, is not a distribution failure at the margin — it is the business model working as intended.

trackers.name: BASF Agricultural Solutions
trackers.desc: WHAT. The agricultural arm of the German chemical group, holding seed and trait assets it bought when competition regulators forced Bayer to divest during the Monsanto acquisition. Runs vegetable seed under Nunhems and field crops including canola and cotton. WHERE IT SITS. Fourth of the four, with a portfolio assembled from what a merger review required someone else to sell. WHY IT MATTERS. The existence of these holdings is the clearest admission on record that competition authorities already regard this as a concentrated market. The remedy — moving assets from the first-largest firm to the fourth-largest — kept the count at four rather than reducing concentration in any meaningful sense.

trackers.name: Rijk Zwaan
trackers.desc: WHAT. A large family-owned Dutch vegetable-breeding company, independent of the four majors, operating worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. Vegetable seed is a separate and highly concentrated market from row crops, dominated by a handful of Dutch and Japanese breeders. WHY IT MATTERS. The vegetable sector shows the same concentration as row crops with almost none of the public attention, and it reaches every kitchen. Most of what is eaten fresh worldwide descends from varieties bred by fewer than ten companies.

trackers.name: Limagrain / Vilmorin
trackers.desc: WHAT. A French agricultural cooperative that owns one of the largest seed businesses in the world, spanning field crops, vegetables and garden seed. WHERE IT SITS. Outside the four majors and comparable in size to them in some segments — evidence that the industry is not quite the four-firm story it is usually told as. WHY IT MATTERS. A cooperative structure means farmer-members own the business, which is often presented as a softer alternative. It has not produced a different position on seed ownership or plant variety rights, which suggests the ownership model matters less than the commercial logic acting on it.

trackers.name: OECD BioTrack
trackers.desc: WHAT. The intergovernmental product database recording approved transgenic products by country, keyed on the OECD unique identifier. WHERE IT SITS. The identifier system the whole industry uses to refer to a specific engineered event. WHY IT MATTERS. Identifiers are assigned to transgenic events. An organism made by mutagenesis or gene editing carries no transgene to name, and generally receives no identifier — so the fastest-growing and least-regulated class of product is also the one this system cannot follow across borders.

trackers.name: Oxford Nanopore Technologies
trackers.desc: WHAT. Maker of portable real-time DNA and RNA sequencers, including a device the size of a phone that costs roughly what a laptop costs. WHERE IT SITS. At the reading end of the supply chain, and the reason reading a genome is now cheap and mobile. WHY IT MATTERS. This is the one part of the industry whose spread genuinely cuts both ways. The same device that lets a company verify its own product lets a community group verify what is in a field. Reading has been democratised. Writing has not, and the asymmetry between those two facts describes the public's actual position better than any argument about biotechnology in general.

trackers.name: Oxitec
trackers.desc: WHAT. Developer of self-limiting engineered insects, principally Aedes aegypti mosquitoes carrying a gene intended to prevent female offspring reaching adulthood. Released in Brazil, the Cayman Islands, Panama, the United States and elsewhere. WHERE IT SITS. The most advanced commercial open-release programme for engineered animals anywhere. WHY IT MATTERS. In Jacobina, Brazil, genotyping after 27 months of weekly releases found DNA from the release strain had entered the wild population. What moved was the strain's background genome rather than the self-limiting transgene, and the company disputes the paper's framing — but the design premise had been that lethality was complete and the population's genetics would be unaffected. Self-limiting was a design claim, and the field tested it.

trackers.name: HFEA — licensed clinic register
trackers.desc: WHAT. The UK regulator's searchable register of every licensed fertility clinic, with inspection findings, licence conditions and outcome data by clinic. WHERE IT SITS. The only clinic-level public accounting of the fertility industry anywhere in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. It demonstrates that clinic-level transparency is achievable, which removes the industry's usual answer that it is not. Everywhere else, a patient choosing a clinic is choosing on marketing. Here they can read the inspection report.

trackers.name: BGI Group
trackers.desc: WHAT. One of the world's largest genomics organisations, running sequencing at enormous scale and manufacturing its own instruments after acquiring Complete Genomics. WHERE IT SITS. The main non-Western pole of the sequencing industry, and a direct competitor to Illumina on instruments as well as services. WHY IT MATTERS. It breaks the assumption that this industry is Western and therefore governed by Western rules. Sequencing capacity at this scale, under a different regulatory and political system, means any framework that only reaches North America and Europe reaches a shrinking share of the field.

trackers.name: CLEA Japan / Japan SLC
trackers.desc: WHAT. Japanese breeders and suppliers of laboratory animals including transgenic and immunodeficient strains. WHERE IT SITS. The regional supply for one of the largest biomedical research bases in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. The animal trade is regional in a way the rest of the industry is not, and each region's practices are governed by its own welfare law. A model developed under one standard is used in publications read everywhere.

trackers.name: Sooam Biotech
trackers.desc: WHAT. A South Korean laboratory offering commercial dog cloning and associated research services. WHERE IT SITS. The other pole of the commercial pet-cloning trade alongside the US operation. WHY IT MATTERS. Pet cloning is the clearest case of engineering-adjacent biotechnology sold direct to consumers with no biosafety framework engaged at any point. It also normalises the practice: an industry that can clone a pet for a paying customer has already answered, commercially, questions that are still being debated formally elsewhere.

trackers.name: Suzano / FuturaGene
trackers.desc: WHAT. The world's largest pulp producer, whose FuturaGene subsidiary developed the first genetically modified eucalyptus approved anywhere, cleared by Brazil's CTNBio in 2015, followed by a glyphosate-tolerant version in 2021. WHERE IT SITS. The only commercial-scale engineered forestry programme approved in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. Post-release monitoring for the approved eucalyptus was compiled from questionnaires filled in by field technicians, in reports authored by the company's own employees and contractors. Self-reported surveillance by the party with the commercial interest is the norm in this industry rather than the exception, and this is the best-documented example of it.

trackers.name: IVIRMA Global
trackers.desc: WHAT. One of the largest fertility clinic networks in the world, formed from the merger of Spain's IVI and the US RMA network, operating across Europe, the Americas and the Middle East. WHERE IT SITS. The consolidated end of assisted reproduction — the chain, not the clinic, is now the decision-making unit. WHY IT MATTERS. Spain is a major destination for cross-border reproductive care because its donor rules and legal framework differ from its neighbours'. Consolidation plus regulatory difference means a chain can route patients to whichever jurisdiction permits what they are buying, which is regulatory arbitrage operating on human reproduction.

trackers.name: CropLife International
trackers.desc: WHAT. The global federation of the pesticide and agricultural biotechnology industry, with national affiliates in most countries. WHERE IT SITS. Brussels, next to the institutions it lobbies, coordinating national bodies that lobby their own governments. WHY IT MATTERS. The national affiliate structure means the same positions arrive in dozens of consultations as though they were locally arrived at. Identifying the affiliate operating in a given country is the fastest way to see who is arguing the industry's case there.
